newsitem.title: FRANCE: Centre-right seen winning French election - poll.
newsitem.headline: Centre-right seen winning French election - poll.

text.p: The ruling centre-right will retain a large majority in France's snap parliamentary election, according to the first survey carried out since President Jacques Chirac called the poll.
The CSA poll released on Tuesday said the ruling coalition would win 332 of the National Assembly's 577 seats to 201 for the Socialists and 20 for the Communists.
The Greens and the far-right National Front would win one seat each.
The centre-right coalition of Prime Minister Alain Juppe held 80 percent of the seats in the outgoing assembly.

The poll of 1,002 adults to be published on Wednesday in the daily Le Parisien was carried out on Tuesday and was the first survey released since Chirac announced the election on Monday. It will be held in two rounds on May 25 and June 1.
The survey said the centre-right and allies would win 43 percent of the vote, only slightly down from 44 percent in the last parliamentary election four years ago.
Socialists and allies would poll 28 percent, up from 20.4 percent, and the Communists wold win a virtually unchanged nine percent.
The National Front would slightly improve its score to 13 percent from 12.7, and ecologists would be down to six percent from 11.1.
The survey said voters were split 44 to 44 percent over whether Chirac was right to call the snap election.

Fifty-seven to 40 percent found unconvincing his statement that an early election was needed to give France a position of strength to join the single European currency, with an overwhelming 81 percent believing the snap poll was a political manoeuvre.
Fifty-eight percent to 37 percent believed it was an admission of failure for Juppe's government.
Another survey, conducted by the BVA polling institute days before the election announcement and released on Tuesday, saw the popularity of both Chirac and Juppe dipping sharply.
It rated Chirac's popularity at 35 percent, down from 39 percent a month earlier. The percentage of people with a poor opinion of the president rose to 57 percent from 55.
Juppe's popularity dropped from 29 percent to 25 percent while the percentage of people with a poor opinion of him rose from 63 to 66 percent.

The percentage of people satisfied with the way the ruling centre-right coalition runs France was steady at 20 percent while those dissatisfied dropped one percentage point to 75 percent, the poll showed.
